source_title: Comprehensive Goat Production Guide — East Africa, Tanzania

chunks.text: Dairy goat breeds in Tanzania: Toggenburg — daily milk yield 1.5-2.5 litres, lactation length 250-300 days, mature doe weight 50-60 kg, buck 60-70 kg, good temperament, moderate heat tolerance. Alpine — daily yield 1.5-3.0 litres, lactation 280-300 days, doe weight 55-65 kg, hardy and adaptable to tropical conditions, good for crossbreeding. Saanen — highest yield 2.0-4.0 litres per day, lactation 250-300 days, doe weight 60-70 kg, but sensitive to heat stress, requires shade and ventilation, white coat susceptible to sunburn. Nubian — daily yield 1.0-2.0 litres, high butterfat 4-5%, long pendulous ears, vocal temperament, good for cheese making due to high fat content. Boer — meat breed, mature buck 80-120 kg, doe 60-80 kg, kid growth rate 150-250 g/day, white body with red-brown head, fast growing. East African local goat — hardy, disease resistant, low input requirement, but low milk yield 0.3-0.8 litres per day, slow growth rate, used primarily for meat and as foundation for crossbreeding programs.

Crossbreeding programs for dairy goats in Tanzania: Use Toggenburg or Alpine bucks on local does for improved milk yield while maintaining local hardiness. F1 crosses typically yield 1.0-1.5 litres per day, an improvement over local 0.3-0.8 litres. F2 and F3 crosses can reach 1.5-2.5 litres per day with proper management. Select breeding does based on: milk yield records, udder conformation (well-attached, teats pointing forward), body condition score at mating (2.5-3.0), and disease resistance. Maintain buck:doe ratio of 1:25 for natural service. Keep breeding records to avoid inbreeding — minimum 2 unrelated bloodlines in herd. Introduce new buck genetics every 2-3 years. Cull does that fail to conceive after 3 mating cycles or produce less than 0.5 litres per day after first lactation.

Complete vaccination schedule for goats in Tanzania: Foot and Mouth Disease (FMD) — vaccine: Multivax P or Polyvalent FMD vaccine, 2ml subcutaneously, vaccinate kids at 4 months of age, booster at 5 months, then revaccinate every 6 months. Contagious Caprine Pleuropneumonia (CCPP) — vaccine: CCPP attenuated vaccine (KEVEVAPI or Vetalogica), 1ml SC, vaccinate kids at 3-6 months, booster not required, revaccinate annually in endemic areas. Peste des Petits Ruminants (PPR) — vaccine: PPR attenuated vaccine (Nigeria 75/1 strain), 1ml SC, vaccinate kids at 3-4 months, booster not required, provides lifelong immunity, revaccinate only in outbreak situations. Anthrax — vaccine: Sterne spore vaccine (live attenuated), 0.5ml SC, vaccinate at 6 months, annual booster required. Blackleg — vaccine: Clostridium chauvoei bacterin, 2ml SC, vaccinate at 4 months, booster at 5 months, annual revaccination. Tetanus — vaccine: Tetanus toxoid, 1ml SC, vaccinate at 4 months, booster at 5 months, annual revaccination. Enterotoxaemia (Clostridium perfringens types C and D) — vaccine: Ovilis C+D or Multivax CD, 2ml SC, vaccinate kids at 8 weeks, booster at 12 weeks, annual revaccination, also vaccinate does 4-6 weeks before kidding to boost colostral immunity. Brucellosis — vaccine: Brucella Rev-1 (where licensed), 1ml SC or conjunctival, single dose at 3-4 months, note: not commonly used in Tanzania due to human health concerns with Rev-1 strain.

Post-vaccination observations and cold chain: After vaccination, observe animals for 30 minutes for anaphylactic reactions (facial swelling, difficulty breathing, collapse). Keep adrenaline (epinephrine) available for emergency treatment (0.1ml per 10kg SC). Mild swelling at injection site is normal and resolves in 3-5 days. Cold chain requirements: PPR vaccine store at -20°C for long-term, 2-8°C for up to 30 days once thawed. FMD vaccine store at 2-8°C, do not freeze. All vaccines: transport in cold box with ice packs, protect from direct sunlight, use within 6 hours of opening multi-dose vial. Record vaccination in animal register: animal ID, vaccine name, batch number, date, dose, route, next due date. Expired or improperly stored vaccines should be discarded — never use vaccines that have been frozen and thawed multiple times.

Deworming protocols for goats — comprehensive guide: Anthelmintic drug classes available in Tanzania: Benzimidazoles (white drenches) — Albendazole 10mg/kg orally, Fenbendazole 10mg/kg orally, Oxfendazole 5mg/kg orally. Macrocyclic lactones (clear drenches) — Ivermectin 0.2mg/kg SC or oral, Moxidectin 0.2mg/kg oral, Doramectin 0.2mg/kg SC. Imidazothiazoles — Levamisole 8mg/kg orally or 7.5mg/kg SC. Salicylanilides — Closantel 10mg/kg oral (specific for liver fluke and Haemonchus). Rotation schedule: use one drug class for 3-4 consecutive treatments, then switch to another class. Example rotation: Treatment 1-2 Albendazole (benzimidazole), Treatment 3 Ivermectin (macrocyclic lactone), Treatment 4 Levamisole (imidazothiazole), Treatment 5-6 repeat cycle. FAMACHA scoring system for targeted selective treatment: Score 1 = red conjunctiva, no treatment needed; Score 2 = red-pink, monitor; Score 3 = pink, treat if other signs present (poor BCS, poor coat, diarrhea); Score 4 = pink-white, treat; Score 5 = white/pale, treat urgently. Only treat animals with FAMACHA 3-5, BCS below 2.5, or visible signs of parasitism to maintain refugia (susceptible parasite population on untreated animals to dilute resistance genes).

Signs of anthelmintic resistance development: Treatment failure — animals show no improvement after correct dose administration, faecal egg count reduction test (FECRT) shows less than 90% reduction for benzimidazoles or less than 95% reduction for macrocyclic lactones. Recurrence — eggs reappear in faeces within 7-14 days of treatment instead of normal 21-28 days. Increasing dose required — needing higher than recommended doses to achieve control. Prevention of resistance: avoid treating entire herd (use FAMACHA/BCS targeting), never underdose (weigh animals accurately), quarantine and treat new animals before introducing to herd, rotate drug classes, maintain clean pasture (move to clean paddock after treatment), avoid treating and immediately moving to heavily contaminated pasture, combine drug classes only under veterinary guidance for known resistant populations.

Bloat in goats — complete guide: Frothy bloat (pasture bloat) — caused by rapid fermentation of lush legume pastures (lucerne, clover, cowpea hay). Microbial action produces stable foam that traps gas. Signs: sudden onset, distension of left flank (tympany), distress, kicking at belly, open mouth breathing, recumbency, death within hours if untreated. Treatment: administer 50-100ml vegetable oil or 100-200ml mineral oil orally as anti-foaming agent using drench gun. Dose: 1-2ml oil per kg body weight. If severe: trocarize with 14-gauge needle or trocar cannula at left flank triangle (point of hip, last rib, transverse processes of lumbar vertebrae). Walk animal to stimulate eructation. Free gas bloat (tympany) — caused by oesophageal obstruction (foreign body, choke), physical obstruction of cardia, or inability to eructate (tetanus). Treatment: pass stomach tube to relieve gas, identify and remove obstruction. Prevention: never turn hungry goats onto lush legume pasture, provide hay before grazing legumes, avoid sudden feed changes, mix legume pasture with grass pasture (minimum 50% grass), use anti-bloat blocks containing poloxalene.

Mastitis in goats — comprehensive guide: Clinical mastitis signs: swollen, hot, painful udder (one or both halves), clotted, watery, or bloody milk, reduced milk yield, sometimes systemic signs (fever >40°C, depression, reduced appetite). Subclinical mastitis: no visible signs, elevated somatic cell count (SCC > 1 million cells/ml), detected by California Mastitis Test (CMT) or electrical conductivity. Common organisms: Staphylococcus aureus (most common, contagious), Streptococcus spp, E. coli (environmental), Mycoplasma spp (chronic, no effective treatment). Treatment: intramammary infusion — Cepravin Dry Cow or Teramycin intramammary, one tube per affected half, strip teat to remove debris, clean teat end with alcohol swab, infuse antibiotic, massage udder upward to distribute. Repeat in 12-24 hours for severe cases. Systemic antibiotics for severe cases: Oxytetracycline LA 20mg/kg IM for 3-5 days. Supportive care: strip udder every 2-3 hours to remove infected milk, hot compresses on swollen udder for 15 minutes twice daily, NSAID for pain (Meloxicam 0.5mg/kg oral or Flunixin 1.1mg/kg IM). Prevention: proper milking hygiene (clean dry hands, strip first streams), teat dipping after milking with iodine-based dip (0.5% available iodine), dry doe treatment with long-acting intramammary antibiotic at drying off, separate kids from does at birth and bottle/hand milk.

Pneumonia in goats — comprehensive guide: Causes: viral — Peste des Petits Ruminants virus (PPRV), Caprine Arthritis Encephalitis virus (CAEV), Parainfluenza-3 (PI-3). Bacterial — Mannheimia haemolytica (most common secondary invader), Pasteurella multocida, Mycoplasma spp. Predisposing factors: stress (transport, overcrowding, weather change), poor ventilation in housing, dusty conditions, concurrent viral infection. Signs: nasal discharge (initially clear, becoming mucopurulent), coughing (dry initially, becoming moist), rapid breathing (>40 breaths/min), laboured breathing with abdominal effort, fever >40.5°C, depression, reduced appetite, head hanging, frothy nasal discharge in severe cases. Treatment: Oxytetracycline LA 20mg/kg IM for 3-5 days (first choice), or Enrofloxacin 5mg/kg SC once daily for 3-5 days, or Tulathromycin 2.5mg/kg SC single dose (long-acting). Supportive: keep warm (especially kids), ensure adequate hydration (oral rehydration if not drinking), isolate from herd, provide good ventilation without drafts, vitamin B complex injection to stimulate appetite. Prevention: adequate ventilation in housing (no ammonia smell), avoid overcrowding (minimum 1.5 sq meters per adult goat), vaccinate against PPR and CCPP, gradual acclimatization after transport, quarantine new animals for 14 days.

Footrot in goats — comprehensive guide: Causative agents: Fusobacterium necrophorum (environmental bacterium) and Dichelobacter nodosus (obligate pathogen, survives <7 days in soil). Both required together for disease. Predisposing factors: wet muddy conditions, prolonged moisture, overgrown hooves, introduction of infected animals. Signs: sudden onset severe lameness (score 4-5/5), foul-smelling necrotic discharge between claws, separation of hoof wall from underlying tissue, underrun sole, in chronic cases — deformed overgrown hooves. Differential diagnosis: foot abscess (single swollen digit, less odor), interdigital dermatitis (mild, no underrun). Treatment: foot trimming to remove all necrotic and undermined horn (expose healthy bleeding tissue), footbath in 10% zinc sulphate solution for 30 minutes, or 10% copper sulphate, or 5% formalin (note: formalin stings on raw tissue). Systemic antibiotics: Oxytetracycline LA 20mg/kg IM for 5-7 days, or Procaine penicillin 22,000 IU/kg IM for 5 days, or Florfenicol 20mg/kg IM single dose. Topical: spray exposed tissue with oxytetracycline wound spray. Housing: keep in dry clean area for 48 hours after footbath. Prevention: regular foot trimming every 6-8 weeks, quarantine new animals for 21 days with foot inspection, footbath after rainy periods, avoid wet muddy paddocks, cull chronic carriers (D. nodosus carriers).

Urinary calculi in male goats (urolithiasis): Caused by mineral imbalance in diet — excess phosphorus relative to calcium, high grain diets, insufficient water intake, alkaline urine pH promoting struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) and calcium carbonate crystal formation. Signs: straining to urinate with little or no urine output, vocalization during urination, restlessness, kicking at belly, tail flagging, dribbling urine, distended bladder palpable on rectal exam, rupture of urethra or bladder in severe cases (sudden relief of straining followed by depression and death). Treatment: if urethra not ruptured — try antispasmodic (Buscopan 0.3mg/kg IV), warm water enema to relax pelvic urethra, ammonium chloride 200mg/kg orally to acidify urine. If blocked more than 24 hours — surgical intervention required (urethrostomy at perineal site or tube cystostomy). Prevention: ensure 2:1 calcium:phosphorus ratio in diet, provide adequate clean water (minimum 4 litres per day), add ammonium chloride 0.5% to concentrate ration for bucks and wethers, limit grain intake, provide free choice grass hay and mineral block. Castrate males after 12 weeks (allow urethra to develop) rather than early castration.
